Whatever task was laid upon me

<sig>a 3</sig>

*[did they not feel ashamed] to express whatever comes to the mouth <note>original: "buccam... venerit," a common Latin idiom for speaking plainly or saying whatever is on one's mind without rhetorical polishing</note> (as the saying goes) in publishing their thoughts? Therefore, since this style of writing is not going to offend the ears of the pious, and the sentiments expressed will bring no small benefit to everyone; it is only right that I bid you to have high hopes for this little book <note>original: "libello," a diminutive of "liber" (book), often used by authors or editors as a gesture of modesty</note>, and that I consider it a proper service both to myself and to your brother. And so, let this book go forth successfully; let it be received, reread, and loved. In the meantime, fare you well, and continue to love me, as you indeed do.*

# TO THE MOST LEARNED AND
## IN EVERY BRANCH OF LITERATURE
### THE MOST ACCOMPLISHED MAN,

->To Lord Bernardino of Ianno,<-
->*patrician of Parma,*<-

### BROTHER ARCHANGELUS,

->Friar Minor, sends greetings.<- <note>original: "Minorita," referring to the Order of Friars Minor, or Franciscans.</note>

---

<margin>D</margin>**IVINE** *providence, reaching all things mightily and disposing them sweetly* <note>A paraphrase of Wisdom 8:1, a common theological reference to God's governance of the world</note>, *most illustrious Bernardino, has decreed to strengthen holy religion not only with the Prophets and the sacred* Christian Doctors; *but also to uniquely adorn it by a certain elegant and more secret way of Theology: so that Piety herself, the origin of all good things, might at last walk as securely among all professors of wisdom as she rests safely among those of her own household. For it was necessary that religion (which is the only path to happiness) should be common not only to* Christian *dogmas, but also to Hebrew ones. With this indeed as a companion and guide, we all may be able to arrive more easily and safely at that blessedness for whose sake we were created, and toward the attainment of which we labor with common zeal. And so* God *Almighty, at the appointed times, [decreed] the divine*

<meta>catchword: Cabalisticum (Cabalistic)</meta>

<summary>This page begins the formal dedication by the Franciscan author Archangelus of Borgonovo to his patron Bernardino Aiano, arguing that divine providence uses both Christian and Hebrew mystical traditions to strengthen religious faith.</summary>
<keywords>Archangelus of Borgonovo, Bernardino Aiano, Divine Providence, Hebrew theology, Christian Doctors, Franciscans, Kabbalah</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication from Brother Archangelus of Borgonovo to Bernardino Aiano. It follows the previous page's discussion of Divine Providence choosing to reveal secret wisdom to strengthen the Christian faith.</meta>

<sig>a 4</sig>

[God] sent down from on high the Kabbalistic spirit, destined to illuminate holy religion among all nations. But since, until these times, the Kabbalistic sun had not yet openly risen for the Latin or Greek peoples: that famous Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a brilliant Renaissance philosopher who sought to synthesize all knowledge and was a pioneer of "Christian Kabbalah."</note>, the glory of Italy and a man of remarkable piety, striving to spread the Kabbalistic light—so very beneficial to religion—from the Hebrews to the Latins, formulated many Kabbalistic conclusions according to his own understanding (which I have very recently explained, and have given to the public printed for common use). 

Moreover, many sayings worthy of note from the more secret theologians were interspersed within his nine hundred conclusions <note>Pico's famous *900 Theses*, which he intended to defend in a public debate in Rome in 1487.</note>, which he left untouched. I, however, although I have been a devotee of the name of Kabbalah <term>Cabala</term> <note>From the Hebrew *Qabbalah*, meaning "received tradition"; a form of Jewish mysticism that Renaissance scholars like Pico believed held hidden Christian truths.</note> for many years, have undertaken such a grave matter not under my own auspices, but under yours, commenting on these things and hoping that divine aid will not be lacking for such a necessary and pious duty. 

But those who bring forth new things are immediately barked at by the rage of a thousand Scyllas and a thousand Charybdises <note>original: "scyllae rabies... charibdes." In Greek mythology, these were two sea monsters on opposite sides of a narrow strait. Here, the author uses them to represent the overwhelming and inescapable attacks from critics.</note>. They are never free from rivals who tear at them with malevolent mouths, pour venom upon them, and spread a blasphemous opinion about them throughout the whole world. These critics surely ought to have considered how much opportunity they provide for heretics and Jews to mock us, when they see those whom they thought were the asserters and defenders of Christian dogma <term>Christiani dogmatis</term> now being refuted and rebuffed; indeed, they rejoice that these men are attacked by their own people, whom...

<meta>catchword: they themselves (ipsi)</meta>

<summary>Archangelus credits Pico della Mirandola with bringing Kabbalistic wisdom to the Latin world and explains his own project of expanding upon Pico's unfinished work despite fierce academic and religious opposition.</summary>
<keywords>Pico della Mirandola, Kabbalah, Christian Kabbalah, 900 Conclusions, religious controversy, Scylla and Charybdis, Christian dogma</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page concludes the dedication by Archangelus of Borgonovo to Bernardino Aiano. It follows the previous page where the author defended the study of Kabbalah against critics who viewed it as a dangerous or unnecessary novelty.</meta>

...they themselves could not hostilely conquer. What doctrine is more fitly established to overcome Jewish non-belief <note>original: "iudaicam perfidiam." A common, though harsh, theological term in this era for the refusal to accept Christ as the Messiah.</note>, and to silence the mouths of heretics, than the science which is called Kabbalah <term>Cabala</term> <note>From the Hebrew *Qabbalah*, meaning "received tradition." Christian Kabbalists believed these secret Jewish teachings proved the truths of Christianity.</note>? 

O, what a crime—which no one has ever shuddered at enough (as is fitting)! I weep that such great glory of the more secret theologians is withering away like little flowers. For they, moved by mercy in times past, prepared with unwearied spirit the noble springs of the gardens and deep wells of living waters for the sheep of the Messiah, Christ. 

But to what protector I should devote these writings, or who might care for these matters, I do not know, unless you, most illustrious Bernardino, show yourself merciful and pious toward them; and thus the more secret theologians will be able to boast that they enjoy the breeze of Parma <note>A reference to Bernardino’s home or influence in the city of Parma.</note>. Therefore, receive most kindly these sayings of the more skilled Kabbalists, restored to light by our own modest exposition and dedicated to you. Engage with them in frequent conversation: let them always be most faithful companions to you, and let them be at your disposal. 

Like Job <note>A biblical figure who lost everything but was eventually restored to even greater wealth.</note>, they have been made rich from poverty, and like Mordecai <note>A Jewish hero in the Book of Esther who rose from humble status to become the king's chief minister.</note>, they have become distinguished from a humble state. They carry within their pockets—like the servant of Abraham <note>Referring to Eliezer, whom Abraham sent to find a wife for Isaac; he brought rich jewelry to win over Rebecca (Genesis 24).</note>—an innumerable supply of jewels, from which your soul, like a Rebecca, may be adorned and distinguished. I pray, therefore, that what Zacchaeus <note>A wealthy tax collector in the Gospel of Luke who welcomed Jesus into his home, leading Jesus to say, "Today salvation has come to this house."</note> was to Christ, you might be to these sacred and more secret theologians, so that through their words, salvation may come to your house in Christ Jesus.

<summary>Archangelus concludes his dedication to Bernardino Aiano, arguing that Kabbalah is the best tool for defending Christianity and asking Bernardino to act as a patron for these "secret" teachings.</summary>
<keywords>Kabbalah, Christian Kabbalah, Bernardino Aiano, Parma, biblical metaphors, Job, Mordecai, Zacchaeus, theology, religious polemics</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page serves as the formal title page and the beginning of the preface for Archangelus of Borgonovo’s work. It follows a dedication to Bernardino Aiano, transitioning from a personal address to a general philosophical and theological defense of the Kabbalah as a form of divine wisdom.</meta>

# ARCHANGELUS
## FRIAR MINOR <note>original: "Minoritae." A member of the Order of Friars Minor, commonly known as the Franciscans.</note>
### OF BORGONOVO IN THE TERRITORY OF
### PIACENZA, ON THE EXPLANATIONS
->**of the principal sayings of the more secret**<-
->**theologians,**<-
->**that is, the Kabbalists.**<-

### *An Apologetic Preface to the Reader.* <note>In this context, "apologetic" refers to a formal defense of a religious or intellectual position against critics.</note>

**A**MONG the so varied and manifold gifts which we have received from God—the best and greatest giver of all good things—dearest Reader, no one who thinks rightly will believe that anything more noble or beneficial has happened to mortals than wisdom. For this governs the whole life of man. It teaches first how the soul is to be formed toward God, and then how the whole of life is to be established. Indeed, wisdom is the knowledge of things divine and human. The former, which deals with divine matters, is received by the heart alone through formed faith <note>original: "fidem formatam." In medieval theology, this refers to faith animated by love or charity, rather than a mere intellectual belief.</note>; the latter, however, which regards internal and external human actions, is passed down to posterity on parchments <note>The author distinguishes between "divine wisdom" (spiritual experience) and "human wisdom" (written laws and science).</note>. This human wisdom disposes the outward and civil life of man, and draws the soul toward the consideration of created things; but the divine is a certain most lively spirit, which cannot be expressed by the killing letter <note>original: "occidente litera." A reference to the Apostle Paul's statement in 2 Corinthians 3:6, "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life."</note>, but is written by the finger of God in the hearts of the faithful, according to that testimony of Jeremiah <note>Hieremias</note>: I, the Lord, will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts <note>Jeremiah 31:33. This verse was central to the idea that true religion is internal and spiritual rather than just a matter of external laws.</note>.

<summary>The title page and opening preface of Archangelus of Borgonovo's defense of Kabbalah, defining wisdom as a gift from God that exists in both human (written) and divine (spiritual/internal) forms.</summary>
<keywords>Archangelus of Borgonovo, Franciscans, Kabbalah, Christian Kabbalah, Piacenza, Divine Wisdom, Jeremiah, Scholasticism</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface where the author discusses the "killing letter" of the law versus the "vivifying spirit." It concludes a scriptural reference from the previous page (Jeremiah 31:33) regarding God's internal covenant.</meta>

& I will be their **God**, and they shall be my people. In the pursuit of grasping this wisdom, among other things that are sought after, I observe that nothing is more desirable, nothing more useful, and likewise nothing more holy, than the way the monuments of the most ancient, orthodox, and more secret <term>Theologians</term> <note>original: "Theologorum." In this context, Archangelus specifically refers to the ancient Kabbalists, whom he views as "secret theologians" whose works are being rediscovered.</note> are now emerging into the light everywhere. For what could have ever been more necessary for the benefit of the <term>Church</term> <note>original: "Ecclesiae."</note>, or for the convenience and progress of students? Indeed, the Church will stand safer and firmer through works of this kind—even by these very minute safeguards—and the talents of these students are always trained toward a better harvest. For antiquity itself possesses I know not what peculiar gift in treating arduous matters and investigating divine affairs, which *Marcus Cicero* <note>The Roman orator and philosopher Cicero.</note> also seems to have understood when, in his inquiries discussing weighty causes, he says:

> *The men who existed in those ancient ages, the closer they were to the birth of the world, the more blessed they were in character and mind.* <note>A paraphrase from Cicero’s "Tusculan Disputations," book 1, section 12. Archangelus uses this pagan authority to argue that older sources are closer to divine truth.</note>

If he seems to have spoken aptly concerning ethnic <note>i.e., Pagan or non-Christian.</note> men, how much more correctly can we affirm this of our own? And even more so of the more secret <term>Theologians</term>, who, in the explanation of the sacred letters, do not delay the reader with various and subtle questions. They do not pursue battles of useless words and superfluous conflicts (from which envy, contention, and slander are accustomed to sprout). Instead, they are entirely occupied with this: to more diligently extract the spirit hiding within the letter of the law like a certain husk <note>original: "corticem." A common metaphor in mystical thought where the literal text is the "shell" or "bark" (cortex) that must be peeled away to reach the spiritual "kernel."</note>, so that they may thus affect the mind, change the perception, lift the soul upward, and finally transform the whole man, as great as he is. And in performing this, they do not anxiously procure outside aids, but following the sentiment of the Apostle, they compare <term>spiritual things with spiritual</term> <note>original: "spiritualibus spiritualia." A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:13, a key verse for justifying the allegorical and mystical interpretation of Scripture.</note>, and they blend together a vast power of the scriptures gathered from every side from the <term>sacred letters</term> <note>original: "sacris literis," referring to the Holy Scriptures.</note> as if from fountains (not without great judgment). Which...

<summary>Archangelus argues that the "secret" theology of the Kabbalists is superior to scholastic debate because it focuses on spiritual transformation and the ancient, original wisdom of the world.</summary>
<keywords>Kabbalah, Christian Hebraism, Cicero, Spiritual vs. Literal, Sacred Scripture, Theology, Antiquity</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's argument for the value of ancient Hebrew scholarship in Christian theology. The previous page ended with a quote from Cicero about the wisdom of antiquity; this page applies that logic specifically to the Hebrew language and the literal interpretation of the Bible.</meta>

For as far as the literal sense is concerned, it must be sought most especially from the Hebrews, since they, being dedicated to this task, have observed it with great care. And for this reason, *Nicholas of Lyra* <note>A 14th-century Franciscan whose Bible commentaries were famous for emphasizing the literal sense and utilizing Jewish sources.</note> almost always followed *Rabbi Solomon* <note>original: "Rabbi Salomonem." This refers to Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki), the most influential medieval Jewish commentator.</note>. 

For just as eyes accustomed to the clearest light see less precisely (as *Plato* says) when injured in darkness, so the eyes of our theologians, having dwelt in the spiritual light of the mystical sense, sometimes perceive dark difficulties less clearly than those who are accustomed to the darkness. <note>The author uses a paradox here: Christian theologians are "blinded" by the bright light of the Gospel, while Jewish scholars, whom he considers to be in "darkness" regarding Christ, have sharper eyes for the gritty, literal details of the Old Testament.</note> For although we have sought this from the Hebrews so that we might prove the mysteries of our faith through them and oppose them when they disagree with us, we will nevertheless note in our own sections many things worthy of knowledge—as if reclaiming them from unjust possessors—sharing them with true Israelites <note>A common early modern term for Christians who believed they were the spiritual heirs of the biblical Israelites.</note>, so that they [the Jews] may not boast of having any good thing that the Church does not possess. 

*Jerome* <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> would have done all these things (as *Pico della Mirandola* <note>The famous Renaissance philosopher who integrated Kabbalah into Christian thought.</note> believes) in his introduction to the Psalms, had he not been so occupied with translating that he had no leisure to interpret the Law of Moses. Others did not touch upon Hebrew literature at all. 

The <term>allegorical sense</term> <note>original: "Allegoricus sensus." A method of interpretation where people or events in the Bible are seen as symbols of deeper spiritual truths.</note> (as we have written elsewhere) relates to the literal sense just as matter relates to form; it is, in a way, a species of it that belongs properly and uniquely to the Sacred Scriptures—namely, that the things being discussed also signify something else. And just as "form" is not seen by us directly, but rather as matter clothed in "accidents" <note>In the philosophy of the time, "accidents" are the outward qualities of a thing (like color or shape), while "form" is its inner essence.</note>—through the consideration of which we are granted the ability to contemplate forms—so too are we carried forward to the allegorical sense (which we do not behold with eyes of flesh) by the help of the literal sense. 

Therefore, allegory is established as the goal of understanding; for which reason it is not appropriate to seek it in everything. For not all things are the "end" or goal of all things; rather, many things have arisen and been established both for the sake of the goal and out of necessity. The beginning of this true and heavenly wisdom is defined as the "fear of the Lord" <note>A reference to Psalm 111:10.</note>. For this gift of God is not sent down into a malevolent soul, nor is that heavenly treasure [poured into] an earthen vessel...

<summary>The author argues that Christian scholars should use Jewish literal interpretations of the Bible as a foundation for their own spiritual allegories. He maintains that while the literal sense is essential, the "allegorical sense" remains the ultimate goal of theological study.</summary>

<keywords>Nicholas of Lyra, Rashi, Plato, St. Jerome, Pico della Mirandola, allegory, literal sense, Hebrew studies, Biblical interpretation, Scholasticism</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's defense of studying ancient Hebrew traditions. Having previously discussed the literal interpretation of the Bible, the author now transitions into the "spirit" of the text and the mystical insights found in Kabbalistic writings, while citing Church law to justify the academic study of these "oriental" languages.</meta>

...is committed, or thrown before swine <note>A reference to the biblical proverb from Matthew 7:6: "Do not throw your pearls before swine."</note>. This spirit is handed down only to the sons of God and citizens of the heavenly kingdom, who can cry from the heart, "Abba, Father" <note>original: "Abba pater." A phrase from the New Testament (Romans 8:15) signifying an intimate relationship with God as a child to a father.</note>. To one it is given in this way, to another in that; only Christ, in whom the fullness of divinity dwelt, received it without measure.

The philosophers and all those who were estranged from God lacked this wisdom. Therefore, they became vain in their thoughts, and their hearts were darkened. They felt their way like the blind along a wall, and like those without eyes, they groped and stumbled at midday as if in the dark—to use the words of *Isaiah* <note>original: "Esaiae." Refers to Isaiah 59:10.</note>. These men were content only with prudence and worldly wisdom. While such wisdom may be great and especially necessary for this kind of domestic and peaceful life, it offers no help in attaining the future life unless heavenly wisdom is added. For *knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up* <note>original: "Scientia enim inflat, charitas autem ædificat." A famous quote from 1 Corinthians 8:1.</note>. If knowledge is supported by charity, then earthly wisdom migrates into the heavenly, and darkness is turned into light.

Therefore, excellent reader, receive from among those whom antiquity commends the sayings of the leading <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition which some Renaissance Christian scholars believed held secrets that could prove Christian truths.</note>, which are like divine utterances. They illuminate a keen intellect and give off the "good odor of Christ." I do not wish to boast too arrogantly here of my own labor or the genius of the authors; indeed, if you look within a little more carefully, I believe you will not find fault with our industry, and you will greatly admire the dignity of the authors.

All these things must be weighed so that we do not err, and so that we do not give the enemies of the Church an opportunity to mock us as if we were ignorant. For this reason, it was most wisely decreed in the <term>Council of Vienne</term> <note>A Church council held in 1311–1312 which, among other reforms, mandated the teaching of Hebrew, Arabic, and Aramaic.</note> (as *Clement* states in the only <term>Clementine</term> <note>original: "Clementina." Referring to the *Clementinae*, a collection of Catholic canon law named after Pope Clement V.</note> decree regarding teachers) that in most major universities—namely **Bologna**, **Paris**, **Salamanca**, and **Oxford** <note>original: "Exoniensi." Although literally "Exeter," in the historical context of this specific decree from the Council of Vienne, it refers to Oxford.</note>—and especially wherever the <term>Roman Curia</term> <note>The administrative and judicial body of the Papacy.</note> happens to reside, schools of study should be established...

<summary>The author argues that while worldly wisdom is useful for daily life, only "heavenly wisdom" (charity and spirit) leads to eternal life. He justifies the study of Jewish Kabbalah and Hebrew by citing a 14th-century Church decree that established language chairs at major European universities.</summary>

<keywords>Kabbalah, Council of Vienne, Clementines, university history, Bologna, Paris, Salamanca, Oxford, spiritual wisdom vs. worldly wisdom</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's argument for the academic study of biblical languages. Having previously established that the "spirit" of the text is reserved for the faithful, the author now lists the specific languages required for this deep study—Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek, and Arabic—and justifies their use by citing the need for faithful translation and the recent revival of these studies as a divine sign.</meta>

...of various languages: **Hebrew**, namely, **Chaldean** <note>original: "Chaldei." In this period, "Chaldean" was the standard term used by scholars to refer to the Aramaic language, particularly the dialects used in the Targums and the Zohar.</note>, **Greek**, and **Arabic**. And he himself assigns the reasons for this, saying: so that the learned may know how to translate faithfully into Latin and teach others, and so that people of various languages might be more easily and better instructed. For the meanings of Holy Scripture are more clearly gathered and more easily persuaded to others in their own mother tongue (as they say) than in a foreign one. 

Nor has God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deus Opt. Max." (Deus Optimus Maximus). A title for the Divine borrowed from Roman inscriptions to Jupiter, frequently used by Renaissance humanists to bridge classical and Christian thought.</note>, raised up so many and such great men in this time of ours who study Hebrew for no reason. I believe He does this so that those mysteries which have remained hidden until now might be brought into the light. For this reason, we ought not to despise such studies, unless perhaps we wish to appear ignorant, providing an occasion for contempt to those who wish to gather the true meanings of Scripture.

But now, most sincere reader, it is time that we defend the truth itself rather than the sayings of men. For your goodness knows full well that in many things *Jerome* <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar responsible for the Vulgate, the standard Latin Bible.</note> disagrees with *Augustine* <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whose theological writings shaped Western Christianity.</note>, and *Scotus* <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Scholastic philosopher known for his complex "Subtle" reasoning.</note> from *Thomas* <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent Dominican theologian.</note> and *Henry* <note>Likely Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a prominent philosopher at the University of Paris whose views often countered those of Aquinas.</note>. For this reason, the oracles themselves <note>original: "oracula." Here referring to the divinely inspired original texts of the Bible.</note> must be diligently inspected and considered with a proper examination, from which (as *Plato* rightly feels) we ought to be taught concerning divine matters. 

It must also be noted that in interpreting the scriptures, we should not be bound to any one person, nor *swear by the words of any master* <note>A famous phrase from the Roman poet Horace: "Nullius addictus iurare in verba magistri." It was a common motto for scholars emphasizing independent thought.</note>, except for the most Holy Church and the Holy Scripture, whose passages (as is the custom of truly wise men) we ought to clarify one by means of another. We should not do this through philosophy, nor through the sayings of those devoted to philosophy; for *Paul* says: *See to it that no one seduces you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition* <note>original: "Videte ne quis vos seducat..." A quote from the New Testament, Colossians 2:8.</note>. <margin>}</margin>

In these things and in all my sayings and writings, I always submit myself to the judgment of the most Holy Roman Church and of skilled men, and I believe nothing beyond or short of what she, my mother the Church, believes. 

Farewell, and pray to God for me.

<summary>The author advocates for the study of biblical languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek, Arabic) to ensure faithful translation and clear understanding of scripture, arguing that the original "oracles" are more reliable than the conflicting opinions of medieval theologians.</summary>
<keywords>biblical philology, Hebrew studies, Scholasticism, Jerome, Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, Duns Scotus, Church authority, translation</keywords>

For whatever animal we offer signifies that our own "animal" <note>The author is using the sacrificial animal as a metaphor for the human physical or "animal" soul.</note> must be offered to God as a spotless sacrifice, pleasing to God, just as Paul teaches the Romans <note>Referencing Romans 12:1: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice."</note>.

-># OF THE CABALISTS<-

...from hearing. Two lambs were to be brought: one in the evening, the other in the morning. The evening sacrifice was performed to appease the accusers appearing before the tribunal of justice; these were those who accused the uncircumcised as being guilty of <term>original sin</term> <note>original Latin: "culpa originali."</note> not yet atoned for. The morning sacrifice, however, was performed to obtain the grace of mercy and piety from the tribunal located in the south, and God required these two lambs to be offered in perpetuity. 

And many other sacrifices were performed. For sacrifices possess a certain symbolic connection both with the one to whom they are offered and with those who are being purified; yet this is so hidden that the human intellect cannot grasp it, even though everyone admits that sacrifices are necessary. For there is a certain natural intermediary, as it were, between God and man. To sacrifice to God (says *Aristotle* in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, and *Proclus* in the book *On Prayers and Supplications*, and likewise *Plato*, *Plotinus*, and *Porphyry*) is as natural to man as lowing is to oxen and barking to dogs. 

And they add further to this: that whoever scorns to perform this act deserves to be cast out from human nature, and the name of "man" should be denied to him. For it is a "proper" attribute in the <term>fourth way</term> <note>original Latin: "quarto modo proprium." In scholastic logic, this refers to a characteristic that belongs to every member of a species, to that species alone, and at all times (such as the human ability to laugh or, in this case, to worship).</note>; for it applies to every man, to man alone, and always. Moreover, the offering of this or 그 sacrifice for this or that atonement, although it is most fitting according to the natural order,

# M Y D O G M A T A

...happens, yet they were instituted by God; since human inquiry is not sufficient to discover those things which God specifically requires for our <term>atonement</term> <note>original Latin: "expiatione." This refers to the process of making amends for sin to restore the relationship with the divine.</note> according to the order of celestial things, involving both the ones to be purified and the purifying sacrifices, so that the celestial powers might be rendered appeased and refrain from the execution of the punishment which the committed sins deserve.

For the blood of animals seems to purge the sin contracted in the flesh from the blood of our own animal nature, according to that saying of the <term>Apostle</term> <note>Referring to St. Paul in Hebrews 9:22: "And almost all things are by the law purged with blood."</note>: "almost all things are cleansed with blood." He says "almost," because earthen and bronze vessels were to be cleansed with water. Nor is it without reason that man—who is the bond of all things, contains all things, and holds a supreme symbol in his <term>lower part</term> <note>In this philosophical context, the "lower part" refers to the physical body or the reproductive organs, through which the "beginning of sin" (original sin) was thought to be transmitted down the generations.</note>, in which and through which the beginning of sin is contracted—was purged along with animals through the blood of unblemished animals, which were offered by the priest of the Law.

Nevertheless, certain other sacrifices existed earlier; for instance, the fruits of the earth and the firstfruits, as is evident from the case of <term>Abel</term> <note>Referring to the biblical Abel, who offered the firstlings of his flock, contrasted here with the "law of nature" offerings of the earth's fruits.</note> and the observation of the <term>law of nature</term> <note>The "lex naturae" is the moral code believed to be inherent in human reason, which guided humanity before God gave the formal "Written Law" to Moses.</note>. ...[intel]lects, they are called separate; yet they are not stripped of matter, as they are called "separate intelligences" in common speech. Hence, the natural philosophers, when describing the breadth of beings, [place] at its peak the <term>pure act</term> <note>original: "actus purus"; a philosophical term for a being who is fully realized and has no potential for change, namely God</note> without matter; at the bottom is <term>matter</term> without <term>form</term>; while all things in between are shown to be a mixture of <term>form</term> and <term>matter</term>. 

Indeed, this matter of the angels is not physical and subject to decay; but just as the matter of the heavens differs from the matter of things that can be born and perish through a certain analogy, so also the matter of angels differs from the matter of others. Hence the ancients—Basil, Origen, and Gregory—and all the Academics <note>The "Academics" here refers to the followers of the Platonic Academy</note> said that angels have bodies. The Hebrews, however, call the first order **Holy Living Creatures** <note>original: חיות קדוש, *Chayot Ha-Kodesh*</note>, which means "animals of holiness" or "lives." Through these angels, God, as **I AM** <note>original: אהיה, *Eheieh*, the name of God revealed to Moses at the burning bush, signifying pure existence.</note>, bestows the gift of being. 

Second, he bestows the **Wheels** <note>original: אופנים, *Ophanim*; often associated with the "wheels" in Ezekiel’s vision.</note>, which are forms or wheels, through which God, as **Elohim** <note>original: אלהים, a name of God emphasizing His role as Judge or Creator.</note>, distinguishes the **Chaos** <term>Chaos: The unformed, void state of the universe before God gave it order.</term>. 

In the third place are the **Valiant Ones** <note>original: אראלים, *Erelim*.</note>, the great, strong, and robust angels. Through these, the **Tetragrammaton** <term>Tetragrammaton: The sacred four-letter name of God (YHWH), often considered too holy to pronounce.</term> pronounced as **Elohim**, or the **Tetragrammaton** joined with the name **Adonai** <note>original: אדני, meaning "Lord."</note>, administers the form of fluid matter. 

In the fourth place are the **Amber-Colored Ones** <note>original: חשמלים, *Chashmalim*; based on the glowing metal seen in prophetic visions.</note>, through whom **Elohe** <note>original: אלוה</note>, the God of bodies, fashions their outward appearances. 

In the fifth place are the **Burning Ones** <note>original: שרפים, *Seraphim*.</note>, through whom God, as **Elohim Gibor** <note>original: אלהים גבור, meaning "God of Might" or "The Mighty God."</note>, brings forth the elements. 

In the sixth place are the **Messengers** <note>original: מלאכים, *Malachim*</note>, that is, angels, through whom God, as **Eloha** <note>original: אלוה</note>, produces metals. 

In the seventh place are the **Divine Ones** <note>original: אלהים, *Elohim*</note>, that is, Gods, through whom the **Tetragrammaton Sabaoth** <note>original: יהוה צבאות, *Yahweh Tzabaoth*, meaning "The Lord of Hosts."</note> produces all things that grow <note>i.e., the plant kingdom.</note>. 

In the eighth place are the **Sons of God** <note>original: בני אלהים, *Benei Elohim*</note>, through whom...

### DOCTRINES.
B
<meta>catchword: se-</meta>

God as **Elohim of Hosts** <note>original: אלהים צבאות, *Elohim Zabaoth*; a name signifying God's mastery over the celestial armies.</note> procreates the living creatures. In the ninth place are the **Cherubim** <note>original: כרובים, *Cherubim*.</note>: through these, God as the **Almighty** <note>original: שדי, *Sadai* or *Shaddai*; a name associated with God’s sufficiency and protection.</note> cares for the human race. Beneath these is the ensouled order <term>Ensouled order: *Ordo animasticus*, referring to a rank of beings or souls that bridge the gap between pure spirit and physical life.</term> called the **Issim** <note>original: אישים, *Issim*; literally "men" or "individuals," often interpreted as the souls of the righteous.</note>, that is, heroes, strong men, and the blessed: through these, God as the **Lord** <note>original: אדני, *Adonai*.</note> bestows the gift of prophecy. 

Our theologians, however, posit three distinctions of angels, and divide each of these into three orders, so that there are three distinctions constituting nine orders, and they call these hierarchies or choirs. In the superior hierarchy, they place the **Seraphim**, **Cherubim**, and **Thrones**, as spirits existing beyond the heavens, contemplating the order of Divine Providence. The first of these focus on God’s goodness; the second on His essence; the third on His wisdom. 

In the middle hierarchy, they place **Dominions**, **Virtues**, and **Powers**, as worldly spirits working together for the government of the world: of which the first give the commands that the others carry out; the second administer the heavens, sometimes reaching out to perform miracles; the third ward off those things that seem able to disturb the divine law. 

In the lower hierarchy, however, they place **Principalities**, **Archangels**, and **Angels**: and these descend to care for the things below. Of these, the first care for public affairs, such as princes and magistrates, provinces and kingdoms, each assigned to their own specific charge.

# DOGMAS

<margin>4</margin>
**The Cabalistic Doctor:** The sin of Adam was the cutting off of the Kingdom from the rest of the plants. <note>original: "truncatio regni à cæteris plantis" — In Kabbalistic thought, this refers to "uprooting the shoots," a metaphor for Adam separating the final divine emanation, Malkuth (Kingdom), from the other Sephirot, thereby disrupting the flow of divine harmony.</note>

**F. A.:** The method of teaching used by the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism. Here, the author explains why they use metaphorical rather than literal language.</note> is through parables, figures, and similarities. For a parable, according to its definition, is a comparison of dissimilar things; for this reason, parabolic speech is effective. First, because it is based on sensible things <note>Things that can be perceived by the five senses.</note>, from which both the ignorant and the learned can gain understanding. This is evident in that famous parable: **A sower went out to sow his seed**; <note>original: "Exijt, qui seminat seminare semen suú" — A reference to the Parable of the Sower found in the Gospels (e.g., Luke 8:5).</note> for everyone understands what a seed is, what a field is, and so on. Second, because stories are more easily imprinted on the mind; for a parable serves as a tool for "artificial memory" <note>A classical system of memory techniques (mnemonics) used to organize and recall information through vivid mental images.</note>. Third, because our knowledge takes its origin from the senses; therefore, it shared a symbolic bond with sensible parables. Fourth, there is great spiritual consolation found in the agreement of a parable with the spiritual reality it represents. For Paul, in agreement with this doctrine, says:

> The invisible things of God from the creation of the world are understood and seen through those things which have been made. <note>original: "inuisibilia Dei à creatura mundi per ea, quæ facta sunt, intellecta conspiciuntur" — A translation of Romans 1:20.</note>

Here, therefore, this doctor, treating the sin of Adam parabolically and learnedly, does not follow the method of our own theologians. The sin of our first parents consists in the fact that they did not obey the Divine command, which was that they should not eat the fruit, or that tree: which tree is the Law. For man, since he was a crea- <note>The text cuts off here, likely intending the word "creature" or "created being."</note>

# CABALISTS

...chiefly from the accidents of the soul <note>original: "accidentibus animæ" — In medieval philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities or states, such as temporary emotions or conditions, rather than the soul's core essence.</note>, namely anger, sadness, joy, and the like. For these are governed by the mind, since all things (as I have said) are placed within its power. Nor should anyone blame their temperament <note>original: "complexionem" — This refers to the "complexion" or the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that was thought to determine a person's physical and mental health.</note>, because, as **Ecclesiastes** says, God made man upright and most balanced <note>original: "temperatiſsimum"</note> in terms of both the body and the <margin>f</margin> soul. Yet man himself entangled himself in infinite questions, or as the Hebrew truth <note>original: "veritas Hebraica" — A scholarly term used to refer to the original Hebrew text of the Old Testament as the ultimate authority over translations.</note> has it: "he himself sought out many schemes" <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 7:29.</note>. 

Thus, not content with the uprightness and perfect state in which the Creator <note>original: "opifex" — Literally "craftsman" or "maker."</note> had placed him, he wandered about many things. From this followed a disturbance of the soul and body, and a complete fallenness from his state and his uprightness. This is most fully shown in the <term>first-created man</term> <note>original: "protopaste" — From the Greek *protoplastos*, referring specifically to Adam as the first human formed by God.</note>, who, not content with the right law which his Maker <note>original: "plasmator"</note> had established for him, began to seek out "truth" <note>Likely referring to the forbidden knowledge of good and evil.</note>, from which that disturbance of the soul followed. And in this temptation, **Adam** was not deceived, but the woman was deceived, as **Paul** says <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 2:14: "And Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression."</note>.

# DOGMATA.

**Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose logic and physics dominated medieval thought.</note> says that species are like numbers: <note>original: "species se habent, sicut numeri." ->OF THE CABALISTS<-

...when its aliquot parts <term>aliquot parts: divisors of a whole number that, when added together, equal that number; in the case of 6, these are 1, 2, and 3</term>—namely one, two, and three—are combined, it results perfectly <note>original: "ad vnguem," a Latin idiom meaning "to the fingernail," implying something is polished or perfectly executed</note> in the number itself. Hence, it is also called **marriage** <note>original: "gamon," from the Greek *gamos*</note> by the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the building blocks of the universe</note>. This is because its parts, when placed alongside one another, give birth to it; and also for the reason that it is procreated from the first even number and the first odd number, as if from a male and female <note>In Pythagorean numerology, even numbers were considered female and odd numbers male; 2 x 3 = 6</note>, by multiplying one into the other. For if you join two times three, or again three times two, the number **six** <term>senarius: the Latin term for the number six or a grouping of six</term> arises from both sides. Furthermore, any of the aforementioned aliquot parts combined make up the Six, such as six times one, three times two, or twice three. Indeed, no number more harmonious than six could be found for the construction of the world, for it consists of the double proportion <note>A ratio of 2:1</note> which they contain most closely within themselves. This proportion moreover is that of four to two; these numbers, when joined together, yield six—something you will scarcely find in other numbers, except those that preserve the nature of the six, such as doubles, triples, and so on.

The number six, being the first **perfect number** <term>perfect number: a mathematical term for a number that equals the sum of its divisors</term>, also suits the supreme **Craftsman God** <note>original: "Opifici Deo"</note> or His creation. Just as nothing is lacking in God, so in the number six—when analyzed through its constituent members—nothing is left over, nothing is missing, nothing exceeds, nothing overflows, nothing flows in, and it requires no external support. This river went out from the place of pleasure <note>original: "loco voluptatis" — a reference to Eden, as the Hebrew 'Eden' translates to 'pleasure' or 'delight'</note> to water paradise and all the blessed ones dwelling there. Furthermore, this river is divided fourfold so that this river of all goodness might flow separately into the earthly man himself—the same river which waters together, in unity, those blessed ones who have been made one with God. 

For it waters us from the East through grace, from the South through knowledge and piety, from the North through chastisement and expiation, and from the West through kind reception. Therefore the rivers run with an everlasting flow to the sea from whence they drew their origin, according to the words of <term>Ecclesiastes: the narrator of the biblical book of the same name, traditionally identified as Solomon</term>:

And a little later:

> *To the place from whence the rivers go forth, they return.* <note>original: "Ad locum vnde exeunt flumina reuertuntur" — Ecclesiastes 1:7</note>

So also all creatures come down from that <term>great supra-worldly sea: in Kabbalistic thought, the 'Great Sea' often refers to the Sephirah 'Binah' (Understanding), the divine source from which all creation flows</term> mentioned above, passing through secondary causes.

This river arises in Africa.

The **Tigris**, however, which goes against the Assyrians, arises in a conspicuous spring on a plain in the region of Greater Armenia. Where it flows more slowly, until the borders of the Medes, it is called the **Diglitus** <note>A Semitic name for the Tigris, related to the Hebrew "Hiddekel"</note>. Afterward, it begins to be called the **Tigris** because it seems to fly like an arrow; for the Medes call an arrow a "tigris." It passes through Zeroada and Tesbites where the swifter <term>Arsanias: a major tributary in the Armenian highland</term> flows into it, and later it merges into the Euphrates.

The **Euphrates** is indeed said to arise in Mount Patiedrus of Greater Armenia. Running through the same region, it distinguishes Greater Armenia from Cappadocia and flows into the Persian Gulf (which is called the **Red Sea** <note>original: "Mare rubrum"; in ancient geography, this term often encompassed the Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean as well as the modern Red Sea</note>).

From this, we can reach no logical conclusion as to how these four rivers might have the same origin, since they appear to arise in most distant places. Therefore, it remains to be said that the sea is the source of those four named rivers. But in that case, there will be no particular place that can be called by us a garden, or a **paradise of delights**, which is inaccessible. Thus, that description of the rivers seems entirely **typological** <note>original: "typica"; meaning symbolic or representative of spiritual truths rather than strictly literal geography</note>, through which are understood...

And because **God** has an infallible knowledge of future contingents, it is because He knows things already done no differently than those yet to be done. And just as He knows things already done infallibly and clearly, so too He knows those yet to be done infallibly. 

And although **God** has infallible and most certain knowledge of future contingents, they nevertheless will occur contingently, and not by necessity: because the **Divine will** determined things contingently; for He was able not to determine them. Therefore, the **knowledge of God** does not impose necessity upon the things known by Him. Therefore, God knows future things contingently and freely. In the **composite sense** <term>composite sense</term> <note>In scholastic logic, "sensu composito" refers to a proposition where the necessity applies to the whole statement together, while "sensu diviso" applies it to the parts. The difficulty lies in this: how the **contingency of things** and **God's infallible knowledge** (or **Providence**) can stand together. **Plato**, in his book *The Republic*, says that in **God** there is both infallible providence and the contingency of things. **Aristotle**, in the 11th and 12th books of his *Metaphysics*, places providence in **God**, citing the Chaldean—that is, the **Hebrew**—fathers. Furthermore, in the second book of his *Ethics*, he asserts the contingency of things, saying: "We are the masters of our own acts." <note>original: "nos ſumus noſtrorum actuum Domini"</note> **Augustine** likewise states: "Nothing is so much in the power of the will as the will itself." And in the **Psalms**: "My soul (that is, my will) is always in my hands." <note>Psalm 119:109. The author glosses "soul" as "will" to support his argument for human agency.</note> 

However, how these two things are compatible with one another—namely, that a contingent event is a matter of **infallible providence** in **God**, and **Fate** in the heavens (as **Plato** feels)—is entirely most difficult. And **Ockham** <note>William of Ockham (c. 1287–1347), a major scholastic philosopher.</note> says that this has not yet been revealed to any mortal. [...measured by] time (namely those things which have a beginning and an end); others by the **everlasting** <term>aevum</term> <note>original: "æuo". And because this eternity is unknown to us, it follows that we do not know how to compare our measure—that is, time—with eternity; nor do we know how to recognize their compatibility or their difference from one another; for eternity is the *simultaneous and total possession* <note>original: "tota poſſeſſio ſimul". Therefore we err when we measure the works of **God** according to time, because we do not know how to harmonize time with eternity. # DOCTRINES <note>original: "DOGMATA"</note>

...is said of itself. Therefore it is essential, and by consequence necessary. Thus, every future thing is necessarily future. To these objections, I respond and say that every **contingent future** <note>An event that may or may not happen, such as a human choice.</note> is contingently future, because whatever is able not to be future is not necessarily future; and that which is not necessarily future is contingently future. 

And I say that a contingent future is contingent both when it is and when it is not—it is able to be. And when it is, it is able not to be. When I am actually writing, it is contingent that I am writing, for I am able not to write; and every contingent future is of this kind. 

Regarding the first argument, it is said that if it is assumed that a contingent future known by God does not happen, then it will also be assumed in reality that God never knew it to be future; and consequently, unless it happens, He is not deceived. For if the thing happens, God knows it contingently (for He could have not known it if His **will** <note>original: "voluntas"</note> had not determined it to be future), and He always knows it as future; but if it should never happen, He did not know it as future. 

Regarding the second, it is said by denying the consequence, for a <term>fallacy of diction</term> <note>original: "fallacia dictionis". A logical error where the phrasing of a statement leads to a mistaken conclusion.</note> occurs there by arguing from the <term>composite sense</term> <note>original: "sensu composito". A logical term where a necessity applies to a whole statement (e.g., "It is impossible for a sitting man to be running at the same time").</note> to a false <term>divided sense</term> <note>original: "sensum diuisum". A logical term where necessity is wrongly applied to the person rather than the state (e.g., "A man who is sitting is incapable of ever running").</note>; for this is necessary in the composite sense: "one who sits does not run." Therefore, this [other] statement would be true: "it is necessary for the one who sits not to run"; for...

We observe that deer, fawns, roe deer, and goats are celebrated extensively in Holy Scripture—not only in the *Song of Songs* <note>original: "canticis"; referring to the biblical book also known as the Song of Solomon.</note>, but in the Law and the hymns of David <note>The Psalms.</note>. In the Law, for instance, it is commanded that the Tabernacle be covered with dyed goat skins. Furthermore, while the kidneys and the fat of any animal are forbidden, deer and roe deer are permitted to be eaten in their entirety as clean animals, as we read in <term>Deuteronomy</term>, where it is said:

> Truly, just as you eat the roe deer, so shall you eat the deer.

And again:

> They shall eat of them, as of the roe deer and the deer;

namely, all their internal parts are eaten, except for the blood; because the soul <note>original: "anima"; used here to mean the vital life-force or "nephesh" which biblical law identifies with the blood.</note> is in it, which must not be eaten along with the flesh. This is because the soul of an animal does not serve as nourishment for a human, but rather leads to his depravity, defilement, and destruction (as they say). In the title of <term>Psalm 21</term> <note>In the Vulgate numbering; this corresponds to Psalm 22 in modern translations.</note>, where our version has *Unto the end, for the morning protection*, the literal truth of the text is: *To the victor, for the doe of the dawn*. <note>The author is comparing the Latin Vulgate translation of the Hebrew title "Ayelet HaShachar" with a more literal interpretation used in Cabbalistic study.</note> In many other places, the prophet [David] celebrates deer so much that we clearly understand they refer to some better and hidden things, just as <term>Origen</term> <note>An influential early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) famous for his allegorical and mystical interpretations of the Bible.</note> [does]...

"When he established the heavens above, and balanced the fountains of the waters: when he surrounded the sea with its boundary, and set a law for the waters, that they should not pass their limits: when he weighed the foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging all things." <note>This is a translation of Proverbs 8:28–30, where Lady Wisdom (Sophia) describes her presence alongside God during the Creation. For it is by Love that contrary elements are joined together so that they may constitute some good thing. According to **Plato**, the elements and all other things were united in ancient <term>chaos</term> <note>The formless state of the universe before the Greek gods or a creator brought order.</note> through friendship and love. 

For this reason, **Anaxagoras** <note>The author likely means Empedocles (c. 494–434 BC), the philosopher famous for the theory that the universe is governed by the two opposing forces of Love (Philia) and Strife (Neikos). Anaxagoras was a contemporary known for the concept of *Nous* (Mind).</note> was pleased to hold that all things were generated and corrupted through "friendship" and "strife." For while there was a universal friendship of all parts, all things were one chaos; but when the friendship of parts of the same kind was tightened and strengthened, those parts were gathered together, and there appeared a plant, or an animal, or some other such thing. However, when that universal friendship was loosened—or rather, when strife was made with all things—these types of parts stood separated from those universals and were united with their own kind.

For **Plato** established two **Venuses**, or Loves, because he had recognized that all good things proceeded from "upright love," while all evil things proceeded from "evil and distorted love," just as **Pausanias** <note>A character in Plato's *Symposium* who delivers a speech distinguishing between "Common Love" (physical attraction) and "Heavenly Love" (the love of the soul and virtue).</note> testifies in the same place, saying: "Since Love is twofold, who would deny there are two Venuses?" One Venus indeed...

And all things are filled with love; nothing is empty of it, just as all things are filled with air, which fulfills the appetite of a nature that abhors a vacuum. For by Love (says <term>Boethius</term> <note>An influential Roman philosopher (c. 477–524 AD); his work "The Consolation of Philosophy" famously describes Love as the "chain" that keeps the universe in order.</note>) the heavens are joined, and the elements agree within composite bodies. By Love animals live together; the city is preserved, and every **Commonwealth** <note>original: "Reſpu." (Respublica)</note> receives its growth. By Love, God built the world and governs it (according to <term>Plato</term>), because the nature of the Good is to spread itself and to love, as <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian who blended Neoplatonism with Christianity, teaching that God’s love is "ecstatic"—meaning it moves God out of Himself to create the world.</note> teaches. Hence Pherecydes the Syrian said that God was transformed into love before He created the world. <term>Empedocles</term> <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed that the forces of Love and Strife govern the universe.</note> also says that the highest intelligible sphere is contained by love. And because God created out of love, He also embraced all things with love and demands love from us, so that, connected to one another by love, we may finally be united with Him through love, that all things may be one, just as they were from the beginning. And the sum of all things that He seeks from us is love itself. Divine love (says Dionysius) did not permit the King of all to remain within Himself without offspring. And just as He spreads Himself through love into all things outside of Himself, so through love He delights to draw all things back to Himself, especially man,

...[the morning star] prevails over the worse part and hostile fortune. <note>The text concludes a thought from the previous page regarding how the light of Venus/Lucifer overcomes darkness or misfortune.</note>

According to the **Kabbalists** <term>Kabbalists: Practitioners of Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism that seeks to understand the relationship between the eternal, infinite God and the finite universe.</term>, however, there are two **Venuses**: **Tipheret** <term>Tiphereth: The sixth Sephirah, meaning "Beauty." It represents harmony and the "Sacred King" or Bridegroom.</term> and **Malchut** <term>Malkuth: The tenth and final Sephirah, meaning "Kingdom." It represents the physical world and the "Bride" or Shekhinah (Divine Presence).</term>. These are said to be two "loves," even if they are one love through their reciprocal interaction. 

For this reason, **Solomon** in the **Song of Songs** <note>original: "canticis"</note> introduces the bridegroom **Tipheret** and the bride **Malchut** speaking to one another, especially in those words: *Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth* <note>Song of Songs 1:2. In Kabbalistic interpretation, this "kiss" represents the union of divine energies.</note>. These are the words of the bride **Malchut** addressing **Tipheret** himself, asking for that dimension <note>or "emanation"</note> so that the gift of the Holy Spirit—or **Binah** <term>Binah: The third Sephirah, meaning "Understanding." In Christian Kabbalah, it was often identified with the Holy Spirit.</term>, which is called the "mouth" of the **Sephirot** <term>Sephirot: The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</term>—might flow into her. 

And although those things within are the same as God, and consequently are always full of Divinity, nevertheless **Malchut** cannot communicate the good influence received from the higher dimensions to created things unless she is commanded to do so by them. This occurs when created things are well-ordered with God through the observance of the commandments. Therefore it is said in **Deuteronomy**: *Keep the commandments, and you will abound in good* <note>Cf. Deuteronomy 28:1-11.</note>—namely, the influence of **Malchut**—but if not, you will be cursed in the city, in the field, etc. 

Whence in the **Song of Songs**, **Malchut**, complaining on behalf of the assembly <note>original: "synagoga." In this context, it refers to the community of souls or the people of Israel.</note>, says: *I am black* <note>Song of Songs 1:5.</note>. The Hebrew text has **Shechorah** <note>original: "שחורה Sechora"</note>, which is the same as the dawn. It comes from **Shachar** <note>original: "Sechar"</note>, which is called the "dawn" <note>original: "aurora"</note>, occurring when the light of the sun begins to appear and the darkness is expelled. The bride **Malchut**, therefore, compares herself to the dawn.

> ...from among your brothers; listen to him. <note>original: "de fratribus vestris, ipsum audite." A completion of the quote from Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses prophesies that God will raise up a prophet like himself from among the people.</note>

Recognizing this very fact, the Baptist said in praise of Christ:

> He who comes after me has been preferred before me, <note>original: "Qui post me venit, hic ante me factus est." See John 1:15.</note> specifically in dignity and divine preordination: the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.

For at that time—that is, before the arrival of Christ—a brother was required to **raise up seed** <term>raise up seed: refers to "Levirate marriage," a custom where a man was obligated to marry his deceased brother's childless widow to continue the family line</term> for a brother who died without children, by taking his brother's wife. If a man refused to do this, his sandals were removed from his feet by his close relatives, and he had to pass through their midst while they struck him with sticks. 

However, John—as a kinsman and relative of Christ—foresaw that Christ would betroth the **Synagogue** <note>The personified community of the Jewish faith.</note>, who was the "wife" of his deceased "brother" **Moses**. Christ would then "raise up the seed of salvation" from her. Therefore, John said:

> I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandals,

meaning he was not worthy to take Christ’s place and raise up the spiritual seed of salvation himself, because this is a work that belongs only to one who is both God and man. He speaks, therefore, of Christ the **Bridegroom** and the **Synagogue**, whom Christ took to himself to raise up the seed of his brother Moses, who died without the "offspring of salvation." This is because, as has been stated elsewhere, no one was saved through the Law of Moses. Therefore, the conclusion states that this signifies the union of *Beth* <note>The Hebrew letter Beth (ב), which means "House," here referring to the House of Israel.</note>, that is, the **House of Israel** or the **Synagogue**.

-># OF THE CABALISTS<- <note>The "Cabalists" (or Kabbalists) were Jewish mystics who sought to understand the hidden meanings of the Torah through various methods, including the study of the numerical values of letters.</note>

They form <term>Shaddai</term> <note>Hebrew: שדי. One of the names of God, often translated as "Almighty."</note> and by permuting the letters in this way, *Shid* [שד] composes the name of the Devil: for *Shid* is a <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Chaldean usually refers to Aramaic, the language of the Babylonian Empire and much of the Jewish mystical tradition.</note> name signifying a Demon. It is explained in another way, and first it must be noted that the numbers of the Hebrews are of two kinds: namely, the "greater" and the "lesser." The first arises from the individual numbers of all the specific letters of a word, so that it is their total sum: just as in this name *Shaddai*, the greater number is 314. <note>In Hebrew Gematria, Shin (ש) = 300, Dalet (ד) = 4, and Yod (י) = 10, totaling 314.</note> The other is the "lesser number," also called the "unequal": which takes a unit from every hundred and a unit from every ten, while leaving a number smaller than ten as it is. <note>This method is known as *Mispar Katan* (Small Number) gematria, where zeros are ignored (e.g., 300 becomes 3, 10 becomes 1).</note> And in this way, *Shaddai* [שדי] signifies 8. Because the letter *Shin* [ש] yields 300, and thus in the lesser number gives 3 (by taking one for each hundred); *Dalet* [ד] gives 4 and remains whole; and *Yod* [י] signifies ten, from which one unit is taken. And so their sum will be 8, and such is called the lesser number.

In a similar way, <term>Satan</term> <note>The Hebrew word for "adversary."</note> and the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>original: "Iod, He, Vau, He." This refers to the four-letter holy name of God, YHWH (יהוה).</note> yield the same lesser number, in this way: *Satan* [שטן], *Shin* [ש] 300 <note>reduced to 3</note>, *Tet* [ט] 9, *Nun* [ן] 50 <note>reduced to 5</note>: all of which yield the lesser number 17. <note>3 + 9 + 5 = 17.</note> The *Tetragrammaton* [יהוה], *Yod* [י] 10 <note>reduced to 1</note>, *He* [ה] 5, *Vav* [ו] 6, *He* [ה] 5. All of which yield the lesser number 17, as I said above. <note>1 + 5 + 6 + 5 = 17. The author is pointing out a numerical equivalence between the name of the adversary and the divine name.</note>

> *Just as the gathering of waters is the righteous man: so the sea, toward which all rivers flow, is Divinity.*

The Sea is a collection of waters. And this is twofold: one kind is below the heaven, and another is above the heaven; between these the mass of the heavens is established. This lowest sea is foul with agitation and tide, and is salty, harmful to man for food and drink, yet fertile for fish; it also produces coral. It is the origin of all sweet rivers and rains that fertilize the regions. Furthermore, its water, passing through subterranean channels to springs, leaves behind its moisture and power <note>original: *virtute*</note>, from which the earth—warmed by the sun's rays—produces metals. However, it receives this fertility from those celestial waters above, of which it is said: *Let the waters creep, or bring forth the creeping thing of a living soul* <note>original: *Serpant, aut producant aquæ serpituram animæ viuentis*. And he has a symbolic link with all things: 
*   With **matter** in his own subject; 
*   With the **elements** in his fourfold body <note>Referring to the four classical elements: earth, water, air, and fire, which were thought to compose the human body.</note>; 
*   With **plants** in his vegetative power; 
*   With **stones** in his mere existence; 
*   With **animals** in his ability to sense; 
*   With **Angels** in his mind and wisdom, or in his understanding; 
*   With the **heavens** in the influx <note>The astrological or spiritual "flowing in" of influence from the stars and higher spheres to the earthly realm.</note> of the higher parts to the lower, and in circular motion—tending back to where he came from; 
*   With **God** in the containment of all things. 

This containment man possesses by a certain **composition** <note>meaning man is made of many different parts joined together.</note>, whereas God possesses it by a certain **simplicity** <note>original: "simplicitate." In theology, "Divine Simplicity" means God is not made of parts but is a single, unified essence.</note>. Hence <term>Mercurius</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed.</note> says: *Man is more excellent than the inhabitants of heaven; or at least he possesses an equal lot.* 

And because in those things that share a symbolic link, the transition is easy, it follows that while man receives vigor and influx from the Angels, he is called <term>seraphic</term>, <term>cherubic</term>, <term>Angelic</term>, and such like, according to the nature of the influx he has received. Therefore, man has a commonality with all these things; and from all of them, he receives **purifications**, **illuminations**, and **advancements**.

But descending to particulars, man receives from the **Angels**, so that he may be a good messenger of God and an interpreter of the Divine mind; from the **Archangels**, so that he may rule over all things over which it has been granted to preside; from the **Principalities** <note>original: "principibus." # OF THE KABBALISTS

However, that instrument through which one makes known to another the things that bubble up in the mind, whatever it may be, is called a **tongue**. This (as Plato and Aristotle say) was given so that, by its auspices, we might express those things which we have conceived in the mind. The fleshy tongue administers a double "food": namely, corporal food for ourselves, and spiritual food for others. Regarding the first, Marcus Varro <note>A celebrated Roman scholar (116–27 BCE) known for his works on the Latin language.</note> says: that the tongue (*lingua*) is so named as if it were "binding food" (*cibum ligans*); for it is seen [turning/rolling] it with...

This is the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God. In the *Sefer Yetzirah*, permutations of three of these letters (Y, H, and W) are used to seal the six directions of space.</note>: through these, the **Seraphim** execute what God entrusts to them. For the <term>Ophanini</term> <note>original: "Ophanini," referring to the *Ophanim* or "Wheels" from Ezekiel’s vision, another high order of angels.</note> (as the more secret theologians say) arrange matter; the **Seraphim**, however, fill all arranged things with warming power and life. For it is their care to fill the whole world and all its parts with their warming power; and for this reason, they have six wings.

**Seraphim** are interpreted as "the burning ones," "the glowing," or "the boiling." Indeed, they will not be like this bodily fire, which is consuming and torturing; but like a supreme or <term>supramundane fire</term> <note>original: "supramundanus ignis." A spiritual fire existing above or beyond the physical world.</note> which inflames, tests, and gives life. For they bring down that supreme fire to the lower realms, giving life to all things and inflaming the hearts of the pious.

And because the Seraphim carry that fire of the Holy Spirit, sometimes taking His place on earth, it is for this reason believed that <term>Origen</term> <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 185–253 AD) known for his complex and sometimes controversial views on the nature of the soul and the celestial hierarchy.</note> said the Seraphim are the Holy Spirit—not indeed in their actual essence, but in their office—just as the Angel appearing to Moses is many times called <term>Adonai</term> <note>Hebrew: "Lord," often used as a substitute for the sacred four-letter name of God, the Tetragrammaton.</note> or God. > The name of the Seraphim signifies a state of being always in motion around Divine things, an ineffable warmth, a sharp and super-fervent heat, an ever-inflexible movement, and a power that leads back the lower ranks. And for these reasons, they correspond with the <term>First Mobile</term> <note>original: "primum mobile". In the traditional Ptolemaic model of the universe, this is the outermost sphere that moves all the lower celestial spheres.</note>. For since it is the first thing that is moved, and that immediately by the First Mover Himself, it is rightly carried always toward that First Mover in its revolution, so that, taking up His commands, it may fulfill all things in the others.

> *Circumcision was given for liberation from the unclean powers, which walked about in a circuit.*

God, proceeding to the institution of sacrifices, commanded many things to be offered for diverse and various **expiations** <term>expiations: acts of atonement or rituals performed to cleanse a person of sin or ritual impurity</term>. It ought not to seem harsh that God is delighted by the shed blood of animals, by roasted or burned flesh, and by the fragrances of these and other things, as is said in many places: *And the Lord smelled a sweet fragrance.* <note>A reference to Genesis 8:21, where God accepts Noah's sacrifice.</note> For this reason, these are held among the greatest **sacraments** <term>sacraments: here used in the older sense of "sacred mysteries" or symbolic signs of a hidden spiritual reality</term>. 

Wherefore, for the explanation of this matter, it must be held that the highest God is delighted by no smells and no tastes, nor is He fed by the bodily foods of animals, or by loaves prepared and smeared with oil, or drenched in fat: although all these things were commanded to be done in the Law <note>The Mosaic Law or Torah.</note>. Rather, this was done as a sign of those things which were truly to be done by **Christ**, and of those things which must consequently be carried out by us: namely, by **mortifying our members** <note>original: "mortificando... membra nostra." A reference to Colossians 3:5; the practice of subduing physical desires and the "old self" through self-discipline.</note> and offering them as an acceptable sacrifice. 

The former [animal sacrifices] bore the figure of these things; and furthermore, they were intended so that those powers which continually accuse us of the crimes we have committed and the good deeds we have omitted before the **tribunal of God** <note>The "Divine Court" where, in Kabbalistic and legalistic theology, accusing spirits (Satan) bring charges against human souls.</note> might be appeased.

Under the Law, no one was justified except for sin contracted through ignorance, or through a **mental slip** <term>mental slip: Latin *surreptio*, a theological term for a sin committed without full deliberation, or a "theft" of the mind by sudden impulse.</term>, and the like. For the law to truly justify a man, it is first necessary that it take away sin and free man from the slavery of sin and from debt. Because, therefore, man was deprived of eternal life on account of **original sin** <term>original sin: the inherited state of sin from Adam's fall.</term>, and on account of **actual sin** <term>actual sin: sins committed by an individual's own choice and action.</term> was bound to the eternal punishment of the senses in hell—and thus subject to God’s wrath and hatred—it was therefore necessary first for him to be absolved and purged from both types of sin. Second, he had to be brought back into the grace of God and rendered pleasing <note>Latin: *gratificari*, to be made acceptable through Grace.</note> to attain eternal life. 

Circumcision, however, could not by its own power absolve one from original sin and its slavery, nor bring him back into God’s grace, nor make him meritorious and worthy of eternal life. For that little skin <note>Original: *pellicula*, referring to the foreskin.</note> which was cut, and that small amount of blood shed in circumcision, was of very low value compared to the soul; wherefore it was not a sufficient price for redeeming the whole man—especially regarding the soul—and thus it could not redeem it, nor free it from debt. Similarly, neither animals immolated under the law, nor sacrifices, nor the other [sacraments] of the old law...

# DOGMAS

...of the archetype. Concerning the bridegroom, Solomon sings in the **Song of Songs**, saying: *My beloved is white and ruddy.* <note>Song of Solomon 5:10. In this mystical interpretation, the "beloved" or bridegroom is identified with the divine emanation or Christ himself.</note> For from these colors, his beauty results; he is called *fairer than the children of men.* <note>Psalm 45:2.</note> Here, Solomon also alludes to the effects which the bridegroom himself works within us. For sometimes he presents himself as **white**, namely through the grace of piety and mercy; but at other times he is **inflamed**, namely by the zeal of justice. Hence, it was not without reason that John said that Jesus came, not in water alone, but in water and blood. <note>1 John 5:6. Water is traditionally associated with the "white" of mercy, and blood with the "red" of justice or sacrifice.</note>

This is also understood regarding the **supreme colors**, about which **Plato** in the *Timaeus* and *Phaedo* (just as he had learned from the ancient theologians) writes most extensively. For on the **right** he is white, by reason of the inflows of grace and mercy; but on the **left** he is ruddy, in respect to the outflows of justice and punishment.

Christ himself, the true bridegroom, indicated this when he said he would say to those who will be on his **right**: *Come, you blessed of my father*—that is, of the <term>Supreme Crown</term> <note>original: "coronæ supremæ".
