**F. A.** The Law is of such great dignity that David says in admiration: *Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law* <note>original: "Reuela oculos meos, & conſiderabo mirabilia de lege tua." This is a quote from Psalm 119:18.</note>. For in the Law are the wonders of the Gospel, with which the Law was pregnant. In the Law, the structure and manner of the world is taught: from where the species of things, their order, forms, matter, and operation come, and what the final end of all things might be. Through the Law we are instructed by which way and by which journey we can proceed toward God. In the same place, we are instructed about the past and future outcomes of things, and that all things happen by the providence of God. 

There we are taught about the agreement and wondrous harmony of things among themselves and with God. Furthermore, the <term>Ideas</term> <note>In this context, "Ideas" refers to the Platonic and Augustinian concept of the eternal, divine archetypes or blueprints of all created things existing within the mind of God.</note> are shown there beyond any controversy; there is such power in them (as <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), an influential Christian theologian who argued that these "Ideas" were essential for true wisdom.</note> rightly perceives) that unless they are understood, no one can be wise. For there, the most hidden <term>intelligences</term> <note>In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, "intelligences" usually refers to spiritual beings, such as angels, who were thought to move the celestial spheres and mediate between God and the physical world.</note> are signified to us, as well as their commerce with us—indeed, even the fellowship of God—and how we might draw Him to ourselves so that we may be filled by Him, and He may act more familiarly with us. 

And (what is even greater) in the Law we are taught how we can be transformed into God Himself and be made gods <note>This refers to the concept of "theosis" or "deification," a mystical doctrine where the human soul reaches such a degree of union with God that it participates in the divine nature.</note>. But these things are revealed in such an occult mystery that those who are unworthy, though seeing, do not see, and hearing, they do not understand. Therefore, the Law teaches us to ascend to God, so much so that the Gospel sends us back to the Law, saying: *If you wish to enter into life, keep* <note>original: "Si vis ad vitam ingredi, ſerua." This is the beginning of Matthew 19:17: "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments."</note>

# TEACHINGS OF THE CABALISTS

Many have wandered into error—indeed, all those whose eyes he himself <note>God, or the Divine Light mentioned on the previous page.</note> had not illuminated. For this reason, Pythagoras commands that no one should presume to speak of Divine things without light; I mean that light of which the Psalm sings: *In your light we shall see light.* <note>Psalm 36:9. This reinforces the idea that human reason alone is insufficient for divine mysteries.</note> Bathed in this light, Adam saw God himself walking at midday; he recognized His voice and rightly perceived the natures of all created things, so that he might impose a fitting name upon each one. The same may be said of the Patriarchs, the prophets, and the Apostles, and so on. All were bathed in that Divine light.

A different reasoning applies to Moses and Hezekiah as to why they acted as they did <note>referring to them hiding their faces or turning away, as discussed on the previous page</note>: namely, humility. Therefore, he who desires his prayers to be heard should hide his face according to their example, deeming himself unworthy. This is read of the tax collector, who was justified by his humility, while the Pharisee was condemned for his pride. For the prayer of one who humbles himself penetrates the heavens; confirming this, the Psalm says: *As one approaches a high* <margin>proud</margin> *heart, God will be exalted* <margin>distanced</margin>. <note>A mystical interpretation of Psalm 64:6-7. The author suggests that a "high" or proud heart causes God to become "exalted" in the sense of being distant or unreachable.</note>

> *No spiritual thing, descending to a lower level, operates without a garment.* <note>original: Nulla res ſpiritualis, deſcendens inferius, operatur ſine indumento. A core Kabbalistic concept: divine energy must be "clothed" in denser forms (like speech, light, or matter) to interact with the physical world.</note>

F. A. <note>Possibly an abbreviation for "Fundamental Article" or a specific author's initials.</note> It is held as a firm foundation that man was formed in the image of God, and thus it is necessary that he enjoy a figure similar to Him. For we attribute limbs to God in a human manner—namely, eyes, hands, and so forth.

# OF THE KABBALISTS

...[these] are the garments <note>original: "indumenta"</note> through which we are able to know God: whom we cannot grasp in His naked and pure essence. The limbs are the manifold powers within that one, most simple Being. And the garments are certain paths through which He pours Himself out into us. While He acts toward us through the limbs—that is, through His manifold powers—in Himself He performs a single, unified action. The Kabbalists <note>Followers of Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism. During the Renaissance, many Christian scholars studied these texts to find deeper meanings in the Bible.</note> discuss these garments in the *Ilan* <note>Hebrew for "Tree," referring to the diagram of the Tree of Life.</note>, or in the Tree of the Sephirot <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself to the world.</note>; for through these garments, every power emanating from Him proceeds. For from the "naked" God—who is entirely removed from every relationship or perspective—nothing flows; for in Himself He contains all things, like a fountain of all goodness. In the act of flowing out, He puts on a certain relationship, which they call a "garment." 

And there are ten such garments. For God is said to be "naked" when He is considered in His naked and pure essence, entirely removed from every relationship, whether arising from within or from without—insofar as He exists here, communicating Himself to no one. In this state, He is called *Ein Sof* <note>Hebrew for "The Infinite" or "Without End," referring to God's essence before any manifestation.</note>, about which mention is made in the conclusions of Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who integrated Kabbalistic ideas into Christian thought.</note>. He therefore, being most high in this state before He interacted with created things, begat the Son, with whom He simultaneously produces the Holy Spirit. <note>The author is interpreting the mystical Hebrew concept of Divine emanations through the lens of the Christian Trinity (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit).</note> Thus, when He begat the Son, He put on the first garment: which in Scholastic <note>The traditional system of theology and philosophy taught in medieval European universities.</note> terms is called "paternity" <note>The state or relationship of being a Father.</note>; and it is called *Keter Elyon* <note>Hebrew for "Supreme Crown," the highest of the ten Sephirot.</note>; and

If He punishes, He puts on justice, etc. This is because it is a contradiction for God to remain solely within Himself and yet create something; for by the act of working, a relationship immediately arises between God and the creature, which (according to <term>Scotus</term> <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a highly influential Franciscan philosopher and theologian.</note>) is a <term>relationship of reason</term> <note>original: "relatio rationis." In traditional philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that is not essential to the nature of a thing, but is associated with it (like the color of a garment compared to the person wearing it).</note>. Likewise, **consonance** <note>original: "consonantia." In this context, it refers to a harmonic agreement or resonance between two things.</note> within things is something implanted by nature and is **consubstantial** <note>Essential to the very being of the object.</note> with the thing itself. Yet, in the way it travels through the air or a medium until it reaches the one perceiving it, it is a certain accident. Thus, an effect proceeds from that substantial thing by means of an accident.

For that consonance is so essential to the thing that it is included in its very definition. Just as **Aristoxenus** <note>Aristoxenus of Tarentum (4th century BC) was a Greek philosopher and music theorist who famously described the soul as a "harmony" of the body.</note>, following the mind of **Plato**, defines the soul by placing a "rational consonance" within it. For he says: *The soul is a number moving itself.* <note>original: "Anima est numerus seipsum mouens." This famous definition explores the idea that the soul is both mathematical (ordered) and the source of its own activity.</note> 

And such **motion** contributes to any action <note>original: "operando." Referring to the act of working or functioning.</note>. For every operation is performed through motion—whether it be generative, corruptive, alterative, or local—as is said by the **natural philosophers** <term>naturalists: those who study the physical world (precursor to modern scientists).</term>. Hence, among other things that contribute to health, **Plato** praises motion above all else. 

We see proof of this even in the earliest stage of life; for to drive away crying and to maintain or restore health, nurses are accustomed to **rock** <note>original: "mouere." Literally "to move."</note> infants lying in their cradles. This motion (as **Plato** states in the book he published, *The Laws*) <note>Plato discusses the benefits of rhythmic motion for infants in Book 7 of *The Laws*, comparing the rocking of a nurse to the soothing influence of music.</note> expels the **fear** that often seizes children and restores a proper **tranquility**. Thus, motion contributes significantly to every operation—unless the one acting is he who acts by **will alone** <note>A reference to God, whose creative "operation" requires no physical effort or motion.</note>. However, those working in ma- <note>The text cuts off here. Based on the catchword, the word is likely "material" or "magic."</note>

<meta>catchword: [ma]gia</meta>

In scholastic and Cabalistic thought, "making" often refers to the shaping of form, which is inherently good.</note> concerns the good, while "to create" <note>Original: "creare." Here used in a specific technical sense where "creation from nothing" involves the emergence of matter or the potential for lack/evil.</note> concerns evil. Whence Isaiah says: **I, making good, and creating evil; making light, and creating darkness**; <note>A variation of Isaiah 45:7. The author uses this to support the linguistic distinction between the two acts of God.</note> which is understood in this way: since "to create" is out of nothing, and terminates in a subject, or matter, which has the character of evil: therefore He is said to be **creating evil**. And since "to make" terminates in the form, which has the character of good: therefore He is said to be **making good**. And so, whatever things decline toward matter have the character of evil, and those which approach closer to the highest form have the character of good. 

Therefore, that soul which is created more from the thicker <note>Original: "crassiori," meaning coarser or more material.</note> part is called bad, while that which is truly from the purer part is called good. And such a good soul comes from the East. For as soon as it was created from <term>Chokmah|The Sephirah of "Wisdom," often associated with the primordial point of light or the East.</term> (the East), and placed in <term>Binah|The Sephirah of "Understanding" or "Intelligence."</term>, it entered into <term>Tipheret|The Sephirah of "Beauty" or "Adornment," representing the heart or central balance of the divine emanations.</term>, without passing through <term>Gevurah|The Sephirah of "Severity" or "Strength," associated with judgment and fire.</term>. This is because it contains nothing of imperfection within itself to be purged by <term>Gevurah</term>. Bad souls, however, make their journey through <term>Gevurah</term>, so that by its fire they may become pure from that dross. And thus the conclusion is clear according to the Cabalists.

## OF THE CABALISTS

**F. A.** Two Worlds are accepted by the Cabalists: the corporeal and the incorporeal, the visible and the invisible, the sensible and the mortal, the material and the ideal. The lower World and the upper World: as they read, *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.* <note>original: "In principio creavit Deus coelum et terram," Genesis 1:1.</note> And so they believe heaven symbolically designates the highest things, and earth the lowest. Interpreting it in this way: "In the beginning God created the highest and the lowest," by which they judge that the highest contains the simple and immaterial World, while this dense and physical <note>original: "commentarium," likely used here to denote the manifest or "composed" world of matter as opposed to the "simple" world of spirit.</note> world contains the lowest. From this, they believe the divine law of *Bereshit* <term>Bereshit</term><note>The first word of the Hebrew Bible, meaning "In the beginning."</note> proclaimed concerning creation began with the very letter *Beth* (ב), which in the art of Arithmetic <note>Referring to Gematria, the practice of assigning numerical values to Hebrew letters to uncover hidden meanings.</note> signifies the number two among the numbers. 

Just as if it were meant to be noted that God created two things principally: the entire supreme World with everything dwelling in it, and the entire lowest World, and all things pertaining to it. For if there were only one, it would have been enough for Moses to have written: *Reshit bara Elohim shamayim ve'aretz.* <note>original: "Reſit bara Elohim ſamaim vearez." This removes the letter Beth (meaning "In") from the first word, leaving only "Beginning."</note> That is, *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.* For that summary of creation could have begun without the letter *Beth* (ב)—which signifies "in"—and the word for "beginning" could have been placed without any preposition. Furthermore, contrary to custom, he added to these two created things two "articles"—that is, the word *Et* (את) twice. <note>In the Hebrew of Genesis 1:1, the word "et" appears before both "the heavens" and "the earth." In Cabala, because *Et* is composed of the first letter (*Aleph*) and last letter (*Tav*) of the alphabet, it represents the totality of existence.</note> These are signs of all-encompassing inclusion, because *Et* (את) is formed...

And **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetica—a body of Egyptian-Greek wisdom texts—is attributed.</note>, in the book where he says that God is hidden and manifest at the same time, says: there is nothing even in bodies which is not God himself: for he alone is all things, bringing forth those which are into the light, and enclosing within himself those which are not. ## DOGMAS

...namely God, the common acting nature, who, being diffused into all things, gives to all the power to act. And thus God is everywhere, and nowhere. From this, **place** can be considered in two ways according to the **theologians**: in one way as it is a certain created thing; and in this way God is in all places, just as He is in all things. In another way, place can be considered according to that which is a container of the thing located. And in this way God, according to His own nature, is nowhere, because He is contained by nothing, but rather He contains and preserves all things. However, according to His **effects**, He is everywhere, because He fills every place with His effects; and according to this mode, it is proper to God to be everywhere: for nothing fills every place with its goodness and effects except God. 

Yet He is nowhere in a <term>containing</term> <note>original: "contentive"</note> way, nor in a <term>circumscriptive</term> <note>original: "circumscriptive"; this refers to the way physical bodies occupy space, where every part of the object corresponds to a part of the space</note> way, because this only applies to physical bodies. Nor is He there in a <term>definitive</term> <note>original: "definitive"; in scholastic philosophy, this describes how a spirit (like a soul or angel) is in a place—it is "here" and not "there," but it doesn't have physical dimensions</note> way, because this belongs to created spirits. The reason is: because both of these modes imply limitation. The first implies the limitation of physical quantity. The second argues for a limitation of essence and power. And according to neither of these two modes can anything be in several places at the same time, and much less everywhere. To be in a place <term>replenishingly</term> <note>original: "repletive"; the specific way God occupies space—not by being "stretched" through it, but by being fully present to every point through His power and essence</note> belongs to God, not according to His essence, but according to His effects (as I have said), and so

These things are evident to those who know mathematics <note>Here "mathematics" refers to Gematria and sacred numerology.</note>.
